newsitem.title: BELARUS: Ford boosting E. Europe profile via Belarus.
newsitem.headline: Ford boosting E. Europe profile via Belarus.

text.p: Ford Motor Co , the world's second-largest automaker, plans to boost its presence in eastern Europe next week by opening a vehicle assembly plant near the Belarus capital Minsk.

"This investment will help us to be a major participant in the region," Wayne Booker, Ford vice chairman, told journalists in a telephone conference from his office at Ford headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan.
"You will see a higher profile for Ford in eastern Europe over the next several years -- there's no doubt about that," he added.

The U.S. automaker is planning to invest only $9.8 million in Belarus for a 51 percent stake in a $19.2 million plant with an annual capacity to assemble 6,000 units of Escort cars and Transit vans from imported kits.
But Ford said the venture, named Ford Union (FU), was full of symbolism and potential. The plant will be located at Obchuck, six km (four miles) northeast of Minsk.

FU's opening ceremony on July 30 will mark the first time that passenger vehicles will be built in Belarus, which became a major manufacturer of agricultural tractors and heavy trucks for the old East bloc.
The Belarus Escorts also will be the first west European cars to be made since the end of communism in the former Soviet Union, where the only foreign brands in production are American and Korean.
The Belarus government took 26 percent of the venture by providing $4 million in facilities and 11 hectares of land, $1 million in cash and a package of tax breaks, Ford said.
The remaining 23 percent is held by Lada-OMC, a Belarus-British venture that imports and services Ford vehicles.

The government package includes a five-year exemption on corporate tax and an indefinite allowance for duty-free imports of equipment and material as well as car bodies and parts that will come in kits for assembly at the plant.
"The duty-free import of kits was key to our decision to invest in Belarus," Neil Campbell, FU's general manager, told Reuters.
But some observers see risks in Ford's advantages.

In the early 1990s, the Hungarian government came under fire from the European Union for a modification in its customs regulations that reduced import duties on commercial vehicles with certain dimensions that applied only to Ford Transits. The government soon rescinded the modification.
FU's deal has attracted no heat yet, but Volkswagen AG's Czech automaker Skoda automobilova AS has complained about government obstacles to its own plans to assemble cars in Belarus.
Recently, though, the Belarus government has softened its stance toward Skoda, which now seems poised to receive similar investment incentives granted to Ford.
FU, which has a 99-year rent-free contract to use the plant's land, already envisions expanding onto an adjacent 41 hectares to raise its annual output to 200,000 units.
"That's a long way off," Campbell said. "But we have the land for full-scale integrated manufacturing operation here if market demand is sufficient."
The modest start in Belarus reflects Ford's relatively conservative approach to central and eastern Europe.

Ford already has invested over $200 million to make auto parts in the Czech Republic and Hungary and vehicles in Poland. But this pales against the billions of dollars committed by rivals Daewoo Group , Fiat SPA , General Motors Corp and VW.
Belarus sells only a few thousand new light vehicles a year, and over 80 percent of FU's output is dedicated for Russia, which has an agreement with Belarus for duty-free trade that covers vehicles.
The agreement, which includes Kazakhstan, has been strained, and Russia has considered value-added tax on Belarus imports. But observers said they expect duty-free trade to continue.

Ford officials also said the company wants to supplement exports to Russia with a vehicle assembly plant there, equipped with body and paint shops, that probably would build the small Fiesta and mid-sized Taurus.
